The University of Rhode Island’s graduate Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Program (INP) provides students with course instruction and research experience from faculty who are conducting cutting-edge science concerning brain functioning across variety of areas from aging, movement, language processing, medicinal plants, and molecular proteins, to the study of brain based disorders including Alzheimer’s disease, ALS, ADHD, Fanconia Anemia, Parkinson’s disease, epilepsy and more.
The INP graduate program offers three options: a Master of Science (M.S.), Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) degree, or a Certificate in Neuroscience.
Please note that the Master of Science offers a thesis or a non-thesis option.
The thesis program requires students to match with a mentor and conduct research (resulting in a thesis), while the non-thesis program does not require a mentor match or thesis, consequently the acceptance rate tends to be higher in the non-thesis program.
Specializations Students can choose to work with INP faculty across a variety of colleges and departments such as the College of Environment and Life Sciences, Engineering, Health Sciences, Pharmacy, Physical Therapy and more.

Program requirements: The Ph.D. program requires successful completion of a qualifying exam or an earned M.S. with thesis in an appropriate discipline, a comprehensive examination, and dissertation defense.
As the qualifying exam is meant to be equivalent to the M.S. degree, the exam must be taken no later than the first semester following the completion of eighteen credits of coursework.
A minimum of 72 credits is required.
Of these, 30 credits must be earned through required coursework, 18 to 28 of which may be earned through dissertation and research credits (NEU 591 and NEU 699).
No more than 28 credits can be earned between NEU 591 and 699.
Up to 30 transfer credits will be accepted for students who have already earned an M.S. degree. (Depending on your previous training and experience, certain requirements may be waived at the discretion of your dissertation committee and the Graduate School.) Required courses include: - NEU 502: Introduction to Neurobiology (4 cr) - NEU 503: Introduction to the Neurosciences (3 cr)

- NEU 504: Neuroethics (1 cr) - NEU 511: Human Neuroscience and Neurology (5 cr) - PSY/STA 532: Experimental Design (3 cr) - NEU 581 and 582: Neurosciences Colloquium (Seminar – 1 cr each) - one additional statistics or computational analysis course (e.g. STA 502, 536, 541, 542, 545) Other requirements: - Two semesters of NEU 591: Special Projects in Neurosciences (Independent Study), one in your primary area of research, and one in a related discipline. - Enrollment in journal club (NEU 587: Seminar in Neurobiology or equivalent with permission) for a minimum of 3 credits - A dissertation proposal and successful defense of dissertation - In the final semester, a formal presentation of thesis research is recommended in 581/582

As such, the faculty in the school of education have spent 8 months re-designing a stand-alone Ph.D. program in Education at the University of Rhode Island.
Faculty have used the “best of” current courses to design a scholarly doctoral program that is more research intensive than the current joint program–which was initially designed to prepare educational practitioners.

The proposed program builds on current strengths (courses, faculty, ongoing research) to produce educational scholars who can solve the most intractable contemporary education problems.
The new program will allow students to develop focused expertise in an area of PreK-20 or adult education settings that aligns with our current graduate program offerings and faculty expertise.
How is this program redesigned?
The proposed curriculum keeps selected existing core courses that introduce students to educational research and inquiry as well as academic reading and writing.
The “new” program increases the number of required research methods courses from 9 to 21 credits to foster in-depth educational research knowledge and skill building.
The new program offers flexible options for students to develop focused expertise (18 credits) in an area whereas the current program limits expertise to three “strand” areas.
Finally, the program requires 12 credits of dissertation research.
The new program will draw from pre-existing courses with only two new proposed courses simultaneously submitted with the new program proposal.
The first course is truly new.

This course tentatively titled “Engaged Research Apprenticeship” will provide a structured opportunity for students to actively engage in research projects that make a difference locally and globally.
We are also in the process of converting a pre-existing special topics course to be a permanent course (EDC 586 – Generalized Linear Models, 3cr).
This proposal aligns with many aspects of the URI mission and new strategic plan.

SOE faculty study educational systems (locally and globally) and are well-poised to train the next generation of education scholars.
